subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for October 14, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopu
sentences: Story 1 is about Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Resuscitation.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in adult cardiac arrest patients, how should we interpret Mechanical compared with manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis?
Eight studies involving 6,847 patients were included.
For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04 to 1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit.
Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: Use this for journal club before practice change; decide whether the measured outcome is important enough for bedside decisions.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

script.heading: Story 2 - Comparative Effectiveness of Phenobarbital vs Diazepam for Alc
sentences: Story 2 is about Comparative Effectiveness of Phenobarbital vs Diazepam for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome..
This is a recent research article from JAMA internal medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Adult inpatients with a primary diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal syndrome present on admission who initiated phenobarbital or diazepam on the day of hospital admission were included, how should we interpret Comparative Effectiveness of Phenobarbital compared with Diazepam for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome?
Among 24 643 patients (median [IQR] age, 45 [35-56] years; 18 511 male [75.1%]), 11 919 (48.4%) received phenobarbital and 12 724 (51.6%) received diazepam on the day of admission.

There were no differences in hospital length of stay (marginal mean, 4.1 vs 4.3 days; marginal mean difference, -0.21 [95% CI, -0.42 to 0.00] days) or invasive mechanical ventilation use (marginal risk, 3.1% vs 2.7%; marginal risk difference, 0.4% [95% CI, -0.7% to 1.4%]) between initiation of phenobarbital vs diazepam.

Secondary outcomes were also not different between phenobarbital and diazepam, except for self-directed discharge, which was more frequent among those initiated on diazepam (marginal risk, 9.5% vs 12.6%; marginal risk difference, -3.1% [95% CI, -4.9% to -1.3%]).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.
For English practice, repeat one academic phrase from each article out loud.

articles.title: Impact of clinical frailty on mortality after elective surgery in patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to critical care: a binational intensive care registry analysis.
articles.summary: Frailty was assessed at ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale and patients categorised as non-frail or frail. The matched cohort comprised 5398 patients (2699 without frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 1-4) and 2699 living with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8)), with good post-matching covariate balance. Frailty was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (matched hazard ratio (HR) 1.66, 95%CI 1.22-2.27, p = 0.001) and higher 1-year mortality (matched HR 1.66, 95%CI 1.47-1.87, p < 0.001). Patients without frailty had higher odds of returning to their pre-admission residence at hospital discharge than patients living with frailty (matched OR 1.45, 95%CI 1.29-1.62, p < 0.001). Increasing numbers of patients aged ≥ 90 years require elective surgery.
